subtopic_detail: Microcytosis with a normal ferritin that has not responded to a long course of oral iron
stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends your general practice frustrated that her blood count has not improved. Her general practitioner started oral ferrous sulfate 6 months ago for anaemia and she has taken it daily without missing doses, confirmed by her partner.

Her periods are regular and she uses three pads a day for 4 days. She eats meat three times a week, has no abdominal pain, no altered bowel habit and no black stools. Her weight is stable and she has had no pregnancies.

Her parents were born in Cyprus. Her father was told once that he was anaemic but was never treated.

Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L (115-155) with a mean corpuscular volume of 64 fL (80-100), mean corpuscular haemoglobin 21 pg (27-33), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2) and red cell distribution width 13.1 per cent (11.5-14.5). Ferritin is 85 micrograms/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 28 per cent (15-45) and C-reactive protein is 2 mg/L (less than 5). Her coeliac serology is negative and her faecal occult blood tests were negative on two occasions.

data_table.Examination: No pallor of the conjunctivae, no hepatosplenomegaly, no jaundice
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), mean corpuscular volume 64 fL (80-100), mean corpuscular haemoglobin 21 pg (27-33), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), red cell distribution width 13.1% (11.5-14.5), ferritin 85 micrograms/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 28% (15-45), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative, two negative faecal occult blood tests

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis with high performance liquid chromatography analysis
options.rationale: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count, a normal red cell distribution width and a normal ferritin that has not responded to 6 months of iron is the pattern of a thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency, and Mediterranean ancestry with an untreated anaemic parent supports it. Electrophoresis with chromatography quantifies haemoglobin A2 and F, which confirms beta thalassaemia trait and allows partner testing before she conceives. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources
Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

options.text: Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose as a single infusion and repeat the count in 8 weeks
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is the right answer for genuine iron deficiency with intolerance or malabsorption of oral iron, but her ferritin and transferrin saturation are both normal, so further iron risks overload without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy to identify an occult gastrointestinal bleeding source
options.rationale: Endoscopic investigation is driven by proven iron deficiency, particularly in men and postmenopausal women, and her iron stores are demonstrably adequate, so the procedures would be investigating a deficiency she does not have. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

options.text: Switch to oral ferrous fumarate taken on alternate days and repeat the count in 12 weeks
options.rationale: Alternate day dosing genuinely improves absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose, but changing the salt or the schedule cannot help when iron stores are already replete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

options.text: Prescribe a levonorgestrel intrauterine system to reduce menstrual loss and review in 6 months
options.rationale: Reducing menstrual loss is appropriate where heavy bleeding is causing deficiency, but three pads a day for 4 days is not heavy, and her iron studies confirm that loss is not the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia has three common causes, iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease, and distinguishing them prevents both unnecessary endoscopy and inappropriate long-term iron therapy. Several indices help: thalassaemia trait produces a mean corpuscular volume that is disproportionately low for the degree of anaemia, a red cell count that is normal or raised rather than reduced, and a normal red cell distribution width, whereas iron deficiency raises the distribution width and lowers the red cell count. The Mentzer index, mean corpuscular volume divided by red cell count, below 13 favours thalassaemia trait and above 13 favours iron deficiency, though it is a guide rather than a rule. Confirmation is by haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography, where a raised haemoglobin A2 establishes beta thalassaemia trait; alpha thalassaemia trait gives normal electrophoresis and needs genetic testing. Identification matters most for reproductive counselling, since two carriers risk a child with transfusion dependent disease, and iron deficiency should be corrected first because it can falsely lower haemoglobin A2.
key_points: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count and normal distribution width suggests thalassaemia trait
A normal ferritin and no response to 6 months of adherent oral iron argues strongly against iron deficiency
Haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography confirms beta thalassaemia trait through a raised haemoglobin A2
Alpha thalassaemia trait has normal electrophoresis and requires genetic testing to confirm
Diagnosis matters mainly for partner testing and reproductive counselling
explanation.pearls: Correct any coexisting iron deficiency before requesting electrophoresis, because iron deficiency lowers haemoglobin A2 and can mask beta thalassaemia trait on the very test used to diagnose it.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

subtopic_detail: Investigating episodic flushing with diarrhoea and a right sided murmur after normal colonoscopy
stem:
A 57-year-old woman attends your general practice with 8 months of episodes in which her face and upper chest become hot and deep red for about 10 minutes. She particularly notices them after red wine.

She also opens her bowels five or six times a day with loose stools and has lost 6 kg without dieting. Her periods stopped 5 years ago and her general practitioner attributed the flushing to menopause, but she notes she does not sweat during the episodes and they never wake her at night.

Her thyroid function is normal, coeliac serology is negative and her faecal calprotectin is within normal limits. A colonoscopy to the terminal ileum 3 months ago was macroscopically and histologically normal. She takes a proton pump inhibitor for reflux.

On cardiac examination there is a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes louder on inspiration, and her jugular venous pressure shows prominent systolic waves. Her liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin and is firm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge increasing on inspiration, prominent systolic jugular venous waves, firm liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function normal, coeliac serology negative, faecal calprotectin within normal limits, colonoscopy to the terminal ileum normal macroscopically and histologically

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum tryptase with a 24 hour urinary methylhistamine collection during an episode
options.rationale: Mast cell activation and mastocytosis produce flushing, but they characteristically cause itch, urticaria and hypotension, and the tricuspid regurgitation and hepatomegaly here point to a different process. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.text: Serum chromogranin A measured while she continues her current proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: Chromogranin A is a useful neuroendocrine tumour marker, but proton pump inhibitors raise it substantially through hypergastrinaemia, so a level taken without withholding the drug for about 2 weeks is uninterpretable. This is the near-miss that fails on drug interference rather than on biology. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.text: A 24 hour urinary collection for fractionated metanephrines and normetanephrines
options.rationale: Catecholamine excess causes episodic headache, palpitations, sweating and hypertension, and flushing in phaeochromocytoma is uncommon, with pallor being more typical during a paroxysm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Repeat follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol with a trial of menopausal hormone therapy
options.rationale: Vasomotor flushing of menopause is accompanied by sweating and night waking and does not cause diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly or a right sided murmur, all of which demand another explanation. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Vasomotor symptoms)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Vasomotor symptoms

options.text: A 24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid collection with the required dietary restrictions
options.rationale: Dry flushing without sweating, secretory diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly and a tricuspid regurgitant murmur together describe carcinoid syndrome with liver metastases and carcinoid heart disease, and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is the established screening test for serotonin overproduction. Dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods such as bananas, avocado, walnuts and pineapple is essential or the result will be falsely raised. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome arises when a neuroendocrine tumour releases serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation, which for a midgut primary generally requires liver metastases, since the liver would otherwise clear the mediators from portal blood. The clinical picture combines dry flushing, secretory diarrhoea that persists with fasting, and in a minority bronchospasm, alongside hepatomegaly from metastatic disease. Carcinoid heart disease affects the right side of the heart because the mediators are inactivated in the pulmonary circulation, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis from fibrous endocardial plaques, and it is a major determinant of prognosis. Screening is by 24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with dietary restriction, followed by cross-sectional imaging and functional imaging with a gallium-68 labelled somatostatin analogue. Somatostatin analogues control symptoms and slow tumour growth, and every patient needs a plan for carcinoid crisis, which can be precipitated by anaesthesia, surgery or tumour manipulation.
key_points: Dry flushing without sweating plus secretory diarrhoea and weight loss should raise carcinoid syndrome
Systemic symptoms from a midgut primary generally imply liver metastases, since the liver otherwise clears mediators
Carcinoid heart disease affects the right heart because mediators are inactivated in the lungs
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid requires dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods to be interpretable
Chromogranin A is falsely elevated by proton pump inhibitors, which must be withheld before testing
explanation.pearls: Cover any anaesthetic, biopsy or interventional procedure in a patient with carcinoid syndrome with an octreotide infusion, because tumour manipulation can precipitate a carcinoid crisis with profound vasodilatory shock that does not respond to catecholamines.

sources.label: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

subtopic_detail: Heart failure with increased wall thickness and low voltage complexes intolerant of standard therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the cardiology ward. A 78-year-old man was admitted 3 days ago with 6 months of worsening exertional breathlessness and ankle swelling, and two episodes of dizziness on standing.

The overnight intern started perindopril and bisoprolol on admission. Both were ceased yesterday after his systolic blood pressure fell to 82 mmHg on standing and he felt faint. He has never been treated for hypertension and his blood pressure has always been recorded as normal in his general practice records.

He had bilateral carpal tunnel releases 6 years ago and has lumbar spinal stenosis.

His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with QRS voltages under 5 mm in all limb leads. Echocardiography reports a left ventricular wall thickness of 16 mm, an ejection fraction of 48 per cent, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction and apical sparing on longitudinal strain imaging. His N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide is 4200 ng/L (below 300 for his age) and his high sensitivity troponin sits persistently at 48 ng/L (below 14) without a rise or fall. His creatinine is 118 micromol/L (60-110).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg supine and 82/56 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasal crackles, pitting oedema to mid shin, no murmur
data_table.Investigations: N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide 4200 ng/L (below 300 for age), high sensitivity troponin persistently 48 ng/L (below 14) with no rise or fall, creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Imaging: Electrocardiogram in sinus rhythm with limb lead QRS voltages under 5 mm; echocardiogram left ventricular wall thickness 16 mm, ejection fraction 48 per cent, grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, apical sparing on longitudinal strain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange invasive coronary angiography to investigate the persistently elevated troponin
options.rationale: A troponin that is persistently elevated without any rise or fall reflects chronic myocardial injury rather than an acute coronary syndrome, and angiography carries contrast nephropathy risk in a man with impaired renal function and no ischaemic history. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Restart bisoprolol at a lower dose and add frusemide, aiming to up-titrate over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Standard heart failure therapy is characteristically poorly tolerated in infiltrative disease, because a stiff restricted ventricle depends on rate and preload, and reflexively re-challenging with a beta blocker repeats the hypotension that already occurred. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Request serum free light chains with urine electrophoresis and bone scintigraphy imaging
options.rationale: Increased wall thickness with paradoxically low electrocardiographic voltages, apical sparing on strain, a history of bilateral carpal tunnel release and intolerance of standard heart failure drugs together describe cardiac amyloidosis. The diagnostic pathway begins by excluding a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis, since a positive result mandates a different workup, and only then does a grade 2 or 3 bone scintigraphy uptake establish transthyretin amyloidosis without biopsy. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Arrange endomyocardial biopsy as the initial definitive investigation of the thickened ventricle
options.rationale: Endomyocardial biopsy remains the reference standard but is reserved for cases where non-invasive testing is equivocal or a plasma cell disorder is present, since the combination of negative light chains and strong bone scintigraphy uptake is sufficient for diagnosis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Arrange exercise stress echocardiography to assess for inducible myocardial ischaemia
options.rationale: Functional ischaemia testing addresses a diagnosis the history does not support and would be poorly tolerated in a man with symptomatic postural hypotension and decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

explanation.summary: Cardiac amyloidosis was long regarded as rare but is now recognised as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction in older adults, particularly the wild-type transthyretin form. The diagnostic clue that should prompt suspicion is a mismatch between marked increase in wall thickness on echocardiography and low or normal QRS voltages on the electrocardiogram, which is the opposite of what hypertensive or hypertrophic disease produces. Extracardiac clues accumulate over years before the cardiac presentation: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis and biceps tendon rupture all reflect amyloid deposition and commonly precede heart failure by 5 to 10 years. Intolerance of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and beta blockers, autonomic features and a persistently elevated troponin without an acute pattern are further pointers. The diagnostic algorithm is sequential and its order matters, since bone scintigraphy uptake cannot be interpreted as transthyretin disease until a monoclonal protein has been excluded, and disease-modifying therapy such as tafamidis is now available for transthyretin cardiomyopathy.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low electrocardiographic voltages is the mismatch that suggests infiltration
Apical sparing on longitudinal strain is a characteristic echocardiographic pattern
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis often precede the cardiac presentation by years
Exclude a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis before interpreting bone scintigraphy
Standard heart failure drugs are often poorly tolerated because the stiff ventricle is preload and rate dependent
explanation.pearls: Digoxin and calcium channel blockers bind avidly to amyloid fibrils and can cause toxicity at ordinary serum concentrations, so both are generally avoided once cardiac amyloidosis is suspected.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

subtopic_detail: Severe abdominal pain with hyponatraemia and proximal weakness after starting a new medication
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward. A 26-year-old woman was admitted 3 days ago with severe generalised abdominal pain and vomiting. She has had 20 mg of morphine over the past 12 hours with little effect and is still rating her pain at 9 out of 10.

Her abdomen is soft with no guarding and bowel sounds are reduced. Computed tomography of the abdomen on admission was normal, her lipase is normal and her pregnancy test is negative. The surgical registrar has found nothing to operate on and has asked for a medical opinion.

She started a combined oral contraceptive pill 4 weeks ago and takes nothing else. She smokes and drinks alcohol on weekends.

Over the past 12 hours she has become intermittently confused and agitated, and the nurses report she now struggles to lift her arms off the bed to hold a cup. The overnight team diagnosed the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and started a fluid restriction.

A nurse mentions that the urine left in the bedpan for a couple of hours has turned a deep reddish brown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 158/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen without guarding, reduced bowel sounds, symmetrical proximal upper limb weakness, intermittent confusion and agitation
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L, lipase within normal limits, pregnancy test negative
data_table.Imaging: Computed tomography of the abdomen on admission reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the fluid restriction at 1 litre daily and recheck the serum sodium in 12 hours
options.rationale: The biochemistry does fit the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, but here that syndrome is a manifestation of the underlying disorder rather than the diagnosis, and fluid restriction with carbohydrate deprivation actively worsens an acute porphyric attack. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

options.text: Give 3 per cent sodium chloride in 100 mL boluses until her confusion improves, then reassess
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is appropriate for seizures or a depressed conscious state from severe hyponatraemia, but her confusion is fluctuating alongside progressive weakness and pain, which points to a neurovisceral process that saline will not treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy to identify a cause not visualised on the initial imaging
options.rationale: Negative laparotomy is a classic feature of the natural history of undiagnosed acute porphyria, and surgery adds anaesthetic agents that are themselves porphyrinogenic to an active attack. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

options.text: Send urine porphobilinogen and start intravenous haem arginate without awaiting the result
options.rationale: Severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, hyponatraemia, confusion, proximal motor weakness and urine that darkens on standing, in a woman 4 weeks after starting an oestrogen-containing pill, is an acute porphyric attack. Urine porphobilinogen confirms it, but haem arginate must not wait for the result because motor neuropathy can progress to respiratory failure within days and is only partly reversible. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Start tolvaptan for presumed inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion and monitor sodium
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonism corrects the sodium without touching the process generating it, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination while the true diagnosis remains unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria results from partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase in the haem synthesis pathway, and attacks are precipitated when demand for haem synthesis rises, classically through oestrogens, cytochrome P450 inducing drugs, fasting, alcohol, infection and stress. The presentation is neurovisceral: severe abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to a soft abdomen with normal imaging, autonomic features including tachycardia and hypertension, hyponatraemia that is usually mediated through inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, psychiatric disturbance, and a progressive motor neuropathy that can reach respiratory failure. Diagnosis rests on a raised urine porphobilinogen on a fresh sample protected from light, and urine darkening on standing is a helpful but late clue. Treatment is intravenous haem arginate with a high carbohydrate intake, removal of the precipitant, and careful attention to which analgesics and antiemetics are safe, since many common drugs are porphyrinogenic. Fluid restriction for the hyponatraemia is actively harmful because carbohydrate deprivation drives the attack.
key_points: Severe pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, plus hyponatraemia and neuropsychiatric features, should trigger the diagnosis
Oestrogens, cytochrome P450 inducers, fasting, alcohol and infection are the usual precipitants
Send urine porphobilinogen on a fresh light-protected sample, but treat before the result returns
Haem arginate with high carbohydrate intake is the treatment; fluid restriction worsens the attack
Motor neuropathy can progress to respiratory failure, so monitor vital capacity during an attack
explanation.pearls: Safe analgesia and antiemesis in an acute attack means morphine, paracetamol, ondansetron and gabapentin, while diclofenac, metoclopramide, phenytoin, carbamazepine and sulfonamides are among the drugs that must be avoided.

sources.label: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

subtopic: Palliative and end of life care
subtopic_detail: Responding to a first formal request for voluntary assisted dying in a neurodegenerative illness
stem:
You are a general practitioner in Victoria making a home visit to a 61-year-old man with motor neurone disease, diagnosed 20 months ago. You have been his general practitioner for 12 years.

He now uses non-invasive ventilation overnight and his forced vital capacity is 42 per cent predicted. His neurologist has documented in a recent letter that death is expected within 8 to 10 months. He has an established relationship with the community palliative care service, which has been involved for 6 months.

He has lived in Victoria for the past 8 years and is an Australian citizen. His cognition is intact on formal testing and a recent psychiatric assessment found no depressive disorder and confirmed intact decision-making capacity.

Sitting with his wife present, he tells you clearly and without prompting from anyone: "I want to make a formal request for voluntary assisted dying." You have not completed the approved assessment training. He asks you what happens next.

data_table.Examination: Generalised wasting with fasciculations, uses non-invasive ventilation overnight, forced vital capacity 42 per cent predicted
data_table.Assessment: Cognition intact on formal testing, recent psychiatric assessment found no depressive disorder and confirmed decision-making capacity
data_table.Eligibility details: Australian citizen, resident in Victoria for 8 years, neurologist documents expected death within 8 to 10 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline the request, because the expected prognosis exceeds the 6 month eligibility limit
options.rationale: The 6 month limit applies to most conditions, but the legislation sets a 12 month limit where the disease is neurodegenerative, and motor neurone disease falls within that provision. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Decline the request, because motor neurone disease is specifically excluded from eligibility
options.rationale: No specific disease is excluded by name; eligibility turns on an advanced, progressive, incurable condition causing intolerable suffering within the relevant prognostic window, which motor neurone disease can plainly satisfy. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Refer him to the palliative care service and revisit this once his prognosis falls under 6 months
options.rationale: He is already under palliative care, and deferring a valid first request until an arbitrary later point risks him losing the capacity that eligibility requires, which is a recognised harm in rapidly progressive neurodegenerative illness. (Source: Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying)
source_refs: Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying

options.text: Advise that Supreme Court approval must be obtained before any assessment can proceed
options.rationale: No court involvement is required; oversight sits with the statutory review board, which reviews each case after the fact rather than authorising it in advance. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Record the request, respond formally within the required period and refer to a trained practitioner
options.rationale: A practitioner who receives a first request must accept or refuse it within 7 days and must document the request and the response in the medical record, and a practitioner who has not completed the approved assessment training cannot act as coordinating practitioner and so must refuse and refer. His neurodegenerative diagnosis brings him within the 12 month prognostic criterion, so the request is not one that can be dismissed on eligibility grounds. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners
Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying

explanation.summary: Voluntary assisted dying is lawful in every Australian state under separate legislation, and the schemes share a common architecture while differing in detail, so the state matters to every answer. The Victorian scheme requires the person to be an adult, an Australian citizen or permanent resident ordinarily resident in Victoria for at least 12 months, to have decision-making capacity, to be acting voluntarily and without coercion, and to have an advanced, progressive, incurable disease causing suffering that cannot be relieved in a manner the person considers tolerable. The prognosis criterion is death expected within 6 months, extended to 12 months for neurodegenerative conditions such as motor neurone disease. The process involves a first request, a first assessment by a coordinating practitioner, an independent consulting assessment, a written declaration witnessed by two people, a final request and an administration decision, with a statutory board reviewing each case. Practitioners may conscientiously object and refuse to participate at any point, and only practitioners who have completed the approved training can undertake the assessments.
key_points: Every Australian state has its own Act; eligibility details differ, so establish the state first
Victorian prognosis criterion is 6 months, extended to 12 months for neurodegenerative disease
A first request must be accepted or refused within 7 days and documented in the medical record
Only practitioners with the approved training may act as coordinating or consulting practitioner
No court approval is needed; a statutory review board provides oversight after the fact
explanation.pearls: Delay is the practical enemy of eligibility in motor neurone disease, because the person must retain decision-making capacity right through to the final request and administration, and bulbar or cognitive progression can remove it within weeks.

sources.label: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners
Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying
